Berlin*{2Berl.|Etymology}The place is first mentioned by this name in the late 12th century (as gml).}The origin is from German nocap1. from German - by the suffix -in.}According to (incorrect) folk etymology,the name is derived from the Bär that is the symbol of the city.}In a popular etymology of Germanists,it is derived from a from Polabian - stem from Polabian ⋆berl- ~ from Polabian tswamp,for which lexical item there is no evidence in Polabian nor in any Slavic language. Closest to that would be an unknown simple of from Proto-Slavic tcave.}Attested vocabulary is from Polabian tswamp,bog. from Proto-Slavic ⋆bělь also meant a “swampy meadow” or “white field”,which fits the location at the ''märkische Streusandbüchse'',the “Margraviate pounce box” notorious for its sandy soil,and is also the noun behind ''Belitz''.é0bɛʁˈliːn,bɛɐ̯ˈliːn,(Standard New High German),}bɐ̠liːn,bɐ̠liːən,(@^isch)}Ⓓ/c/c0/De-@^-2.ogg(@^,standard)(@^,standard)}Ⓓ0/0e/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ0/06/De-@^2.ogg`9toponym,,@^,plural:[@^@^])}#Place caplc/and/state}#}@^ '''@^''' ist mehr ein Weltteil als eine Stadt.}•'''@^''' is more a part of a world than a city.}#}'''1910''',Karl Scheffler,author of ''@^:Ein Stadtschicksal'':}#}:'''@^''' ist eine Stadt,verdammt dazu,ewig zu werden,niemals zu sein.+'''@^''' is a city damned forever to become,never to be.}#metonymically @^ Literally:[federal government of Germany]|Meronyms}col-auto:Reinickendorf|Derived terms}col-auto:Westberlin,West-@^|See also}table:Germany/de

Bielefeld*!0unk:de. There has been published a multitude about the etymology and it depends on whether early occurrences of resembling toponyms refer to this location,the oldest a ''Bylanuelde'' farmland conveyed to w:Corvey in the mid 9th century,next a ''Biliuelde'' in the w:langde from the 1160s relating occurrences between 1015 and 1036,then a 12th century ''Bylivelt''; only in the 13th century the name of the town occurs clearly and oftener,following which the foundation year is conventionally reckoned the year 1214. A recent overview of the theories is given by Meineke 2013. The areal extent of the city to which the term refers derives from incorporations in 1900,1907,1930,and w:1973.é0ˈbiːləfɛlt}Ⓓ9/91/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ5/55/De-@^2.ogg`9#Place independent city|Derived terms}@^er}@^erin

Bienenstich*!0Biene,(bee)Stich,(sting). Its origin is unclear. Various theories have been proposed. The most common theories are:}Stich could also mean "stocked up mass". Compare Eierstich.}According to folk etymology,in 1474 the citizens of the city Linz am Rhein planned an attack on its neighboring city Andernach because its most imported source of income,collecting tariffs for the transportation of goods on the Rhine river,was revoked by the emperor and granted to its neighboring town. In the next morning,two baker apprentices from Andernach named Fränzje and Döres walked along the city wall and ate from the beehives. As soon as they saw the attackers,they threw the beehives at them. Stung by the bees,the attackers from Linz were forced to retreat. Birne*£3 bire,£9 bir,`b bira,`b pira,from German pira,reanalysis of the plural of from Latin pirum. Early Modern German  is from the Middle High German plural and dative/genitive singular,whence a double plural  was formed. The contemporary  is a new backformation from this plural (perhaps influenced also by the older,still dialectal form ). Thus,between Latin and modern German,the word was reformed on the basis of the plural three times. Brautlauf*!H brūtlouft,reanalyzed as @-4,(bride)Lauf,(run) walk. This reanalyzation is etymologically correct since Old High German ''-louft'' is derived `b loufan (modern laufen). The formation is of from Proto-Germanic - origin:compare from Old Saxon brūdloht,from Middle Dutch bruloft (whence modern from Dutch bruiloft),and slightly differing from Old English brȳdhlop,from Old Norse brúðhlaup (whence from Swedish bröllop,from Danish - and from Norwegian - ''bryllup''). The semantics behind this compound are uncertain. Proto-Germanic from Proto-Germanic ⋆hlaupaną probably meant “to leap,jump”,which would point to the wedding celebration (compare from Dutch huwelijk). However,the sense “to run” may also be old,in which case a reference to the taking-home or ritualized abduction of the bride becomes very suggestive. The latter idea is preferred in much of the literature.é0/ˈbʁaʊ̯tˌlaʊ̯f/£7[Bräutläufe])}#obsolete wedding}•synononym:Hochzeit
